The Reserve Bank of India's revised Integrated [Ombudsman](/tag/ombudsman) Scheme (RB-IOS), 2026 came into effect on July 1, replacing the 2021 framework. The new scheme seeks to strengthen customer protection by providing a faster, cost-free and non-adversarial mechanism to resolve complaints against banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), prepaid payment instrument issuers, payment system participants and credit information companies.  
  
**What is the [RBI](/tag/rbi) Integrated Ombudsman Scheme?**  
The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is a grievance redressal mechanism operated by the RBI that allows customers to file complaints against regulated financial entities if they face deficiencies in service. The scheme follows the "One Nation, One Ombudsman" principle, meaning customers do not have to identify a specific ombudsman office based on geography.  
  

Advt

**Which entities are covered under the scheme?**  
The scheme covers commercial banks, regional rural banks, scheduled and certain co-operative banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers, payment system participants, credit information companies and other regulated entities notified by the RBI under the framework.  
  
**Why did the RBI introduce a new scheme in 2026?**  
The RBI replaced the 2021 framework to strengthen customer grievance redressal, improve operational efficiency, clarify complaint procedures and expand the powers available under the scheme. The revised framework is intended to provide a more effective, transparent and consumer-friendly grievance resolution mechanism.  
  
**Do customers have to approach their bank or NBFC first?**  
Yes. Before approaching the RBI Ombudsman, customers must first lodge a complaint with the concerned regulated entity. Customers can approach the RBI Ombudsman only if the entity does not respond within 30 days, or within the timeline prescribed by the RBI, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) or card network rules, or if the customer is dissatisfied with the response received.  
  
**How long does a customer have to approach the Ombudsman?**  
A complaint can be filed with the RBI Ombudsman within 90 days of receiving the regulated entity's final response or after the expiry of the prescribed response period if no reply is received.  
  

Advt

**What kinds of complaints can be filed?**  
Customers can file complaints relating to deficiencies in service, including unauthorised transactions, ATM and card disputes, digital payment failures, delays in refunds, loan servicing issues, credit report errors, disputes over charges and fees, deposit account problems, payment settlement failures, harassment by recovery agents and other customer service deficiencies.  
  
**What complaints cannot be filed?**  
Certain complaints are not maintainable under the scheme. These include commercial decisions such as loan sanction or pricing decisions, matters already pending before courts or tribunals, anonymous complaints, complaints filed without first approaching the regulated entity, employee-employer disputes, vendor-related disputes and matters involving policy decisions or suggestions.  
  

Advt

**What is the role of RBI Deputy [Ombudsmen](/tag/ombudsmen) under the new scheme?**  
One of the key changes in the 2026 scheme is the expanded role of RBI Deputy Ombudsmen. They can examine complaints relating to deficiencies in service, reject complaints that do not satisfy maintainability criteria, facilitate settlements between parties and assist in expediting complaint resolution. Deputy Ombudsmen also have the power to close complaints falling under specified provisions of the the scheme.  
  
**Does a customer need a lawyer to approach the Ombudsman?**  
No. The scheme is designed to be simple and non-adversarial. Customers may represent themselves or appoint an authorised representative, subject to the conditions prescribed under the scheme.  
  

Advt

**How much compensation can the RBI Ombudsman award?**  
The RBI has enhanced the compensation limits under the new scheme. The Ombudsman can award compensation of up to Rs 30 lakh for consequential financial losses arising from a deficiency in service. In addition, compensation of up to Rs 3 lakh can be awarded for loss of time, expenses incurred, harassment and mental anguish. Under the previous 2021 framework, the corresponding compensation limits were Rs 20 lakh and Rs 1 lakh, respectively.  
  
**Is there any limit on the value of disputes that can be brought before the Ombudsman?**  
No. While there is a cap on the compensation that can be awarded, there is no monetary limit on the value of disputes that can be brought before the Ombudsman under the scheme.  
  
**Can the Ombudsman direct a bank or NBFC to take action?**  
Yes. If the Ombudsman finds a deficiency in service, it can direct the regulated entity to rectify the deficiency, perform specific obligations, refund money, pay compensation or take other remedial measures. The Ombudsman may also facilitate a settlement between the parties.  
  
**Can banks and customers appeal against Ombudsman decisions?**  
Yes. Both regulated entities and customers can appeal against an Ombudsman award within the prescribed timelines. The Appellate Authority is the Executive Director in charge of the RBI's Consumer Education and Protection Department or any other officer of equivalent rank authorised by the Governor of the RBI. However, regulated entities cannot appeal in cases where an award has been passed due to their failure to furnish satisfactory and timely information or documents.  
  
**How can customers file a complaint?**  
Complaints can be filed through the RBI's Complaint Management System (CMS) portal, by email or by submitting a physical application to the [Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre](/tag/centralised+receipt+and+processing+centre) (CRPC) established by the RBI in [Chandigarh](/tag/chandigarh).  
**Is there a helpline for customers?**  
Yes. The RBI operates a dedicated contact centre through the toll-free number 14448, which provides guidance in multiple Indian languages on filing complaints and understanding the grievance redressal process.  
  
**What is the biggest takeaway from the new Ombudsman scheme?**  
The biggest change is that the RBI has attempted to make customer grievance redressal more structured, faster and consumer-friendly by increasing compensation limits, strengthening the role of Deputy Ombudsmen, establishing a centralised complaint processing mechanism and clarifying complaint procedures.

# RBI's new Ombudsman regime set to push banks to step up tech-driven grievance redressal

The Reserve Bank of India's revamped Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, which came into force on July 1, is expected to push banks and other regulated entities to strengthen their internal grievance redressal systems as the central bank seeks faster resolution of customer complaints and greater accountability for service deficiencies.

| RB-IOS 2026 expands the unified grievance redressal framework across banks, NBFCs, PPI issuers and other regulated entities.   Banks will need to improve first-level complaint resolution and strengthen internal grievance systems.   Customer service is set to become a key governance and regulatory focus for lenders.   Technology-led grievance management could emerge as a competitive differentiator for banks. |

  
The new Reserve Bank–Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS), 2026 replaces the 2021 framework and expands the grievance redress architecture across banks, eligible non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers, payment system participants and credit information companies. The scheme aims to provide a cost-free, expeditious and non-adversarial mechanism for resolving complaints related to deficiency in service.  
  
For banks, however, the changes go beyond compliance. Industry experts say the revised framework is likely to make customer service a more closely monitored operational function, requiring lenders to improve complaint handling, strengthen internal ombudsman mechanisms and invest in technology to identify and resolve grievances before they escalate to the RBI.  
  

Advt

The revised scheme forms part of the RBI's broader effort to improve consumer protection amid rising digital banking adoption, increasing complaints related to digital transactions and growing complexity in financial products. Over the past year, the central bank has also reviewed the [Internal Ombudsman framework](/tag/internal+ombudsman+framework), expanded the scope of entities covered under the grievance mechanism and undertaken campaigns to reduce complaint pendency.  
  
**Greater focus on first-level resolution**  
  
The revised framework is expected to increase pressure on regulated entities to resolve complaints at the first point of contact.  
  
Customers must continue to approach the regulated entity before escalating a complaint to the RBI if they do not receive a satisfactory response within the prescribed period. This means banks that improve turnaround times and complaint quality could reduce the number of cases reaching the Ombudsman while also lowering regulatory scrutiny.  
  
Industry executives expect banks to invest more in complaint analytics, artificial intelligence-based categorisation of grievances and centralised monitoring systems to identify recurring service failures.  
  
Wider regulatory coverage  
  
The new scheme also broadens the categories of regulated entities covered under a unified grievance redress mechanism.  
  

Advt

Apart from commercial banks, the framework covers eligible cooperative banks, regional rural banks, deposit-taking NBFCs and specified non-deposit-taking NBFCs, prepaid payment instrument issuers, payment system participants and credit information companies, giving customers a single grievance redress framework across much of the financial system.  
  
**More than a compliance exercise**  
  
The RBI has increasingly emphasised customer protection as a supervisory priority. Recent regulatory actions, including penalties for deficiencies in customer service, KYC compliance and fair practices, suggest that grievance management is becoming an important indicator of governance standards.  
  

Advt

For banks, this means customer complaints are no longer merely an operational issue but increasingly a board-level governance metric. Institutions with stronger complaint resolution systems are likely to face lower regulatory risk, while persistent service deficiencies could attract greater supervisory attention.  
  
With digital banking becoming the dominant mode of customer interaction, the revised Ombudsman framework is expected to accelerate investments in [customer service technology](/tag/customer+service+technology), internal controls and complaint governance, making [grievance redressal](/tag/grievance+redressal) a competitive differentiator rather than just a regulatory requirement.

was launched on 12.11.2021 in virtual mode by Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. The Scheme integrates the existing three Ombudsman schemes of RBI namely, (i) the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006; (ii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies, 2018; and (iii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions, 2019. The Scheme, framed by the Reserve Bank in exercise of the powers conferred on it under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (10 of 1949), Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (2 of 1934), and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (51 of 2007), will provide cost-free redress of customer complaints involving deficiency in services rendered by entities regulated by RBI, if not resolved to the satisfaction of the [...] The Executive Director-in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department of RBI would be the Appellate Authority under the Scheme. Complaints can continue to be filed online on  Complaints can also be filed through the dedicated e-mail or sent in physical mode to the ‘Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre’ set up at Reserve Bank of India, 4th Floor, Sector 17, Chandigarh - 160017 in the format. Additionally, a Contact Centre with a toll-free number – 14448 (9:30 am to 5:15 pm) – is also being operationalised in Hindi, English and in eight regional languages to begin with and will be expanded to cover other Indian languages in due course. The Contact Centre will provide information/clarifications regarding the alternate grievance redress mechanism of RBI and to guide [...] It will no longer be necessary for a complainant to identify under which scheme he/she should file complaint with the Ombudsman.
   The Scheme defines ‘deficiency in service’ as the ground for filing a complaint, with a specified list of exclusions. Therefore, the complaints would no longer be rejected simply on account of “not covered under the grounds listed in the scheme”.
   The Scheme has done away with the jurisdiction of each ombudsman office.
   A Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre has been set up at RBI, Chandigarh for receipt and initial processing of physical and email complaints in any language.

# Banking Ombudsman

The Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (the Scheme) was launched on 12.11.2021 in virtual mode by Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. The Scheme integrates the existing three Ombudsman schemes of RBI namely, (i) the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006; (ii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies, 2018; and (iii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions, 2019. The Scheme, framed by the Reserve Bank in exercise of the powers conferred on it under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (10 of 1949), Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (2 of 1934), and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (51 of 2007), will provide cost-free redress of customer complaints involving deficiency in services rendered by entities regulated by RBI, if not resolved to the satisfaction of the customers or not replied within a period of 30 days by the regulated entity. In addition to integrating the three existing schemes, the Scheme also includes under its ambit Non-Scheduled Primary Co-operative Banks with a deposit size of ₹50 crore and above. The Scheme adopts ‘One Nation One Ombudsman’ approach by making the RBI Ombudsman mechanism jurisdiction neutral. Some of the salient features of the Scheme are:

*   It will no longer be necessary for a complainant to identify under which scheme he/she should file complaint with the Ombudsman.
*   The Scheme defines ‘deficiency in service’ as the ground for filing a complaint, with a specified list of exclusions. Therefore, the complaints would no longer be rejected simply on account of “not covered under the grounds listed in the scheme”.
*   The Scheme has done away with the jurisdiction of each ombudsman office.
*   A Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre has been set up at RBI, Chandigarh for receipt and initial processing of physical and email complaints in any language.
*   The responsibility of representing the Regulated Entity and furnishing information in respect of complaints filed by customers against the Regulated Entity would be that of the Principal Nodal Officer in the rank of a General Manager in a Public Sector Bank or equivalent.
*   The Regulated Entity will not have the right to appeal in cases where an Award is issued by the ombudsman against it for not furnishing satisfactory and timely information/documents.

The Executive Director-in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department of RBI would be the Appellate Authority under the Scheme. Complaints can continue to be filed online on https://cms.rbi.org.in. Complaints can also be filed through the dedicated e-mail or sent in physical mode to the ‘Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre’ set up at Reserve Bank of India, 4th Floor, Sector 17, Chandigarh - 160017 in the format. Additionally, a Contact Centre with a toll-free number – 14448 (9:30 am to 5:15 pm) – is also being operationalised in Hindi, English and in eight regional languages to begin with and will be expanded to cover other Indian languages in due course. The Contact Centre will provide information/clarifications regarding the alternate grievance redress mechanism of RBI and to guide complainants in filing of a complaint.:

[**Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme**](https://financialservices.gov.in/dfs/sites/default/files/media/2026-01/RB-IOS-2021_0.pdf)

# Step-by-Step Procedure for Filing Complaints with the Banking Ombudsman

Last updated on:

When a bank ignores your complaint, delays your refund, or simply refuses to address a legitimate concern, it can feel like you have nowhere to turn. But Indian banking customers have a powerful – and completely free – recourse available to them: the [Banking Ombudsman](https://cms.rbi.org.in). Governed under [the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021](https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/content/pdfs/RBIOS2021_amendments05082022.pdf) (RB-IOS 2021), this mechanism allows customers to escalate unresolved banking grievances to a senior RBI-appointed authority – without any legal fees or court proceedings. But before you can knock on the Ombudsman’s door, there is a specific procedure you must follow. Here’s exactly how it works.

#### Table of Contents

* [What is the Banking Ombudsman?](#what-is-the-banking-ombudsman)
* [When can you approach the Banking Ombudsman?](#when-can-you-approach-the-banking-ombudsman)
* [Grounds for filing a complaint](#grounds-for-filing-a-complaint)
* [Step-by-step procedure for filing a complaint](#step-by-step-procedure-for-filing-a-complaint)
* [Step 1: Approach your bank first](#step-1-approach-your-bank-first)
* [Step 2: Prepare your complaint](#step-2-prepare-your-complaint)
* [Step 3: Submit your complaint](#step-3-submit-your-complaint)
* [Step 4: Initial scrutiny](#step-4-initial-scrutiny)
* [What happens after the complaint is accepted?](#what-happens-after-the-complaint-is-accepted)
* [What if you’re unhappy with the Ombudsman’s decision?](#what-if-youre-unhappy-with-the-ombudsmans-decision)
* [Complaints that will not be entertained](#complaints-that-will-not-be-entertained)
* [The importance of internal resolution first](#the-importance-of-internal-resolution-first)

## What is the Banking Ombudsman?

The Banking Ombudsman is a quasi-judicial authority established by the [Reserve Bank of India (RBI)](https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/Complaints.aspx) under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. First introduced in 1995 and significantly revised through the Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006, the mechanism was further consolidated into the **Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021**, which merged three earlier ombudsman frameworks – for banks, NBFCs, and digital transactions – into one unified system.

The scheme covers all scheduled commercial banks, regional rural banks, and scheduled primary cooperative banks across India. The Ombudsman acts as a neutral mediator: receiving complaints, facilitating conciliation between the bank and the customer, and issuing binding awards where necessary. Importantly, [the service is completely free of charge](https://cleartax.in/s/banking-ombudsman) – no filing fees, no legal representation required.

## When can you approach the Banking Ombudsman?

You cannot directly approach the Banking Ombudsman the moment a problem arises. The scheme requires you to first exhaust your bank’s internal grievance mechanism. Specifically, you are eligible to file a complaint with the Ombudsman only if:

* You have already lodged a complaint with your bank and have **not received a reply within 30 days**, or
* You are **dissatisfied with the bank’s response** to your complaint.

This “bank-first” requirement serves a dual purpose – it gives banks an opportunity to resolve issues at their own level, and it reduces unnecessary burden on the Ombudsman’s office. Additionally, the complaint must be filed **within one year** of receiving the bank’s final response, or within **13 months** of first raising the issue with the bank – whichever comes first. Complaints filed beyond this window are generally not entertained.

## Grounds for filing a complaint

Not every banking grievance qualifies for the Ombudsman’s intervention. Under the scheme, the complaint must relate to a **deficiency in banking services**. Common grounds include:

* Non-payment or unreasonable delay in payment or collection of cheques, drafts, or bills
* Refusal to open a deposit account or close an account without valid reason
* Non-acceptance of small denomination notes or coins without sufficient cause
* Delay or failure to issue drafts, pay orders, or banker’s cheques
* Levying charges without adequate prior notice
* Complaints from NRIs regarding remittances from abroad, deposits, or related banking matters
* Non-adherence to RBI directives on interest rates or any other banking service
* Failure to follow [Banking Codes and Standards Board of India (BCSBI) guidelines](https://www.indiainfoline.com/knowledge-center/financial-planning/banking-ombudsman-redressal-for-customer-complaints-against-banks)

If your complaint falls outside these specified grounds, the Ombudsman is not the appropriate forum and you may need to approach the RBI’s Customer Service Department or a consumer forum instead.

## Step-by-step procedure for filing a complaint

### Step 1: Approach your bank first

Your first step is to formally raise the grievance with your bank. This can be done in writing by emailing the bank’s branch or customer care, visiting the branch in person, or writing to the bank’s **nodal officer**. As per RBI directions, every bank is required to appoint a nodal officer at its head office and senior-level officers at controlling offices to handle customer grievances. Keep a copy of your complaint and any acknowledgment or response you receive – this documentation is critical for the next step.

If the bank does not respond within 30 days, or if you are dissatisfied with the response, you may proceed to the Ombudsman.

### Step 2: Prepare your complaint

Once you’ve established the bank’s failure to resolve your issue, you need to prepare your complaint for submission to the Banking Ombudsman. While there is no mandatory format, [the RBI requires certain minimum details](https://www.business-standard.com/finance/personal-finance/facing-bank-issues-here-s-how-to-file-a-complaint-with-the-rbi-ombudsman-124052700222_1.html) in every complaint:

* **Personal details:** Full name, age, gender, postal address, email ID, and mobile number
* **Bank details:** Name and address of the bank branch or office against which the complaint is made
* **Transaction details:** Account number, debit/credit card number (where relevant), transaction date, and a clear description of the facts giving rise to the complaint
* **Prior correspondence:** Date of the complaint made to the bank, and the bank’s reply (if any)
* **Loss details:** The nature and extent of the loss or harm caused

The complaint can be submitted in **any language listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution**, making the process accessible across India’s diverse linguistic landscape. Crucially, the complaint must be **signed by the complainant or an authorized representative** – though representation by an advocate is not permitted at this stage.

### Step 3: Submit your complaint

Once your complaint is ready, you have two modes of submission:

**Online:** The preferred and most convenient route is the [RBI’s Complaint Management System (CMS) portal](https://cms.rbi.org.in). You fill in the complaint form, select the relevant Banking Ombudsman office based on jurisdiction, and can upload supporting documents directly. Once submitted, you receive a reference number to track your complaint’s status in real time.

**Physical/Email:** You can also submit a written complaint letter to the **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre (CRPC)** at the Reserve Bank of India, or email it to [crpc@rbi.org.in](mailto:crpc@rbi.org.in). Physical complaints must be accompanied by copies of all earlier correspondence with the bank.

An important jurisdictional note: complaints must be filed with the Banking Ombudsman office that has **territorial jurisdiction over the bank branch** where you hold your account or where the disputed transaction took place. The RBI maintains [offices across the country](https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/AboutUsDisplay.aspx?pg=BankingOmbudsmen.htm), with 22 regional offices to ensure accessibility.

### Step 4: Initial scrutiny

After submission, the complaint goes through an initial scrutiny to verify that it is complete, falls within the Ombudsman’s jurisdiction, and satisfies the pre-conditions (i.e., prior bank complaint + 30-day wait or dissatisfaction). Incomplete complaints or those falling outside the scheme’s purview may be rejected at this stage – but you will be informed of the reasons and any alternative remedies available to you.

## What happens after the complaint is accepted?

Once accepted, the Banking Ombudsman will first attempt to **settle the dispute through conciliation** – essentially facilitating an agreement between you and the bank. If conciliation fails to produce a resolution within one month, the Ombudsman proceeds to pass an **award**. Before doing so, both parties are given a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

The compensation that can be awarded is the **lower of the actual loss suffered** or a specified monetary limit. In cases involving [mental agony and harassment, compensation of up to ₹1 lakh](https://cleartax.in/s/banking-ombudsman) may additionally be awarded. The entire resolution process typically takes 30 to 45 days, though complex cases may take longer.

### What if you’re unhappy with the Ombudsman’s decision?

If you are not satisfied with the award passed by the Banking Ombudsman, you have the right to **appeal to the Appellate Authority** – a Deputy Governor-level official at the RBI – within **30 days** of receiving the award. The Appellate Authority may grant an extension of another 30 days if it is satisfied with the reason for delay. If even this recourse does not yield a satisfactory result, you retain the option to pursue the matter in a civil court.

## Complaints that will not be entertained

Knowing what the Ombudsman will not take up is just as important as knowing the procedure. Complaints are typically rejected if:

* The subject matter has already been settled or is pending before another court, tribunal, or forum
* The complaint is frivolous or not made in good faith
* It pertains to matters outside the specified grounds under the scheme
* The prescribed time limit for filing has expired
* The complaint involves a loan or advance amount exceeding a specified limit

## The importance of internal resolution first

The mandatory “bank-first” approach embedded in this procedure is not just a bureaucratic hurdle – it reflects a deliberate policy design. Banks in India are required by RBI to maintain robust internal grievance redressal mechanisms, including dedicated customer care helplines, branch-level complaint registers, and escalation to nodal officers. [Exhausting these internal channels before escalating to the Ombudsman](https://www.wintwealth.com/blog/banking-ombudsman-scheme-here-is-how-to-file-your-complaint-against-your-bank/) often leads to faster resolution – sometimes in days rather than weeks – and it fulfills the procedural prerequisite that makes your Ombudsman complaint maintainable.

In practice, maintaining clear written records of every interaction with your bank – dates, names, email threads, complaint reference numbers – significantly strengthens your complaint when you do reach the Ombudsman’s office.

**What do you think?** If a bank resolves your complaint just before the 30-day window closes, does that truly constitute a satisfactory resolution – or should the quality of the resolution also be a criterion for approaching the Ombudsman? And given that the entire process is free and accessible online, why do you think a significant number of bank customers still hesitate to escalate unresolved grievances?

Someone who is officially appointed to investigate and resolve your complaints against banks, NBFC's or payment system operators without charging you a single rupee. Without this scheme, it would be time consuming, expensive and honestly overwhelming for most people to fight these big institutions. Earlier we had three ombbudsman schemes. You had the banking ombbudsman scheme of 2006. You had the NBFC ombbudsman scheme of 2018. And you had the digital transactions ombbudsman scheme of 2019. Now this created a lot of confusion in public. Which scheme uh you know which scheme uh do one use? Uh what if you know the complaint uh involved both a bank and a wallet? Now to fix this in November 2021 the RBI basically integrated these three schemes into one integrated omudsman scheme. Now you don't have to figure out which scheme or which office to go to whether your issue is with a bank or an NBFC or even a digital wallet provider. There's just one platform, one procedure and zero hassle. Now coming to what does the scheme cover? Then it is also multilingual. That means complaints now are accepted in any Indian language making the process inclusive as well as accessible for all citizens. Then you have centralized processing at RBI Chandigar. All complaints are first rooted to a dedicated center at RBI's Chandigar office ensuring that you know there's quick and uniform processing and obviously there is simplified grounds which is deficiency in service. If you're unsatisfied or you do not get any response then in that case you can escalate this matter to your ombudsman right then you can lodge your complaint either through the website or through a toll-free number or you can uh write to the RBI's Chandigar processing center right the documents which will be required would be your original complaint as well as communication that you had with the bank your account details right or any of the transaction details and then your ID as well as address proof right the important timelines is once you have I mean you can only escalate it to the omudsman after you've waited for 30 days right if you have not gotten a response from the bank then you have 1 year and 30 days to basically escalate this matter or complain or basically escalate this complaint to the ombudsman Right? It is a reasoned written decision that clearly states what the complaint was, what the facts were found, uh what laws or rules were applied and why the ombbudsman decided in favor of one party. Filing a Complaint with the RBI
Below is a step-by-step guide to escalate your grievance—from your bank’s own channels up to the RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme—so you can recover your funds and interest.
1. Exhaust Your Bank’s Grievance Process
Before approaching the RBI, you must first use the bank’s internal channels:
Call the bank’s 24×7 customer helpline and note the complaint reference number, date and time.
If no resolution in 10 days, escalate to the bank’s Nodal Officer (contact details on their website).
If still unresolved in 30 days, escalate to the Principal Nodal Officer.
Keep copies of every email, chat transcript or letter sent, and any reply received.
2. Approach the Banking Ombudsman
If your bank has not resolved your complaint within 30 days or you’re dissatisfied with their response, you can file with the RBI’s Banking Ombudsman under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021: Online via CMS Portal
Go to [https://cms.rbi.org.in](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcms%2Erbi%2Eorg%2Ein&urlhash=VcRR&trk=public_post-text) and click File a Complaint.
Select “Bank” as the entity, fill your details, attach your complaint letter and all supporting documents, and submit.
By Email
Send your complaint to [crpc@rbi.org.in](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=mailto%3Acrpc%40rbi%2Eorg%2Ein&urlhash=ct5H&trk=public_post-text)
Include:
Your name, address, contact number
Name of the bank and branch
Account number and nature of grievance (e.g., forced closure, non-payment of interest).
Dates and copies of all prior communications By Post
Download Annexure A from the RBI website and post to: Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre 4th Floor, Reserve Bank of India Sector-17, Central Vista, Chandigarh – 160017
You’ll receive an acknowledgment within 14 days. The Ombudsman will investigate and issue a decision within 30 days thereafter.
3. What to Include in Your Complaint
Clear statement of facts (when you applied for re-KYC, when account was closed).
Copies of your DigiBank chat transcripts, emails, branch correspondence.
Bank’s communications about interest non-payment.
Proof of balances standing to your credit at closure.
4. After the Ombudsman’s Decision
If the Ombudsman rules in your favour, the bank must comply within 30 days.
If you disagree with the Ombudsman’s order, you may appeal to the RBI Appellate Authority within 30 days of the decision.
5. Additional Options
Cyber Cell Complaint: File an online complaint with the Cyber Cell of the state where you live, if you are a victim of cyber fraud or phishing, identity fraud
Police Complaint: If you suspect willful fraud or negligence, register an FIR at your local station.
Legal Notice: Engage a lawyer to send a formal demand notice to the bank.
Consumer Court: For claims or recovery you may file a legal case in the District Consumer Forum.
Taking these steps will ensure your grievance is escalated through every available channel and documented with the RBI.
Good luck reclaiming your funds.

Have you ever heard of Off-Balance Sheet activities?
While studying the course Commercial Banking and Risk Management, this question came to my mind and pushed me to explore it further.
Off-balance sheet items are those assets or liabilities that do not appear on the bank’s balance sheet, yet they carry potential risks and obligations. These include instruments like letters of credit, guarantees, derivatives, and securitized assets.
At first, they seem harmless and even useful, as they help banks manage risk and improve liquidity. But when misused, they can become the hidden channels for major financial frauds.
A real-life example that caught my attention was the [Punjab National Bank](https://in.linkedin.com/company/pnbindia?trk=public_post-text) (PNB) fraud of 2018. Employees issued unauthorized Letters of Undertaking (LoUs), which are off-balance sheet instruments, without proper approvals. This led to a fraud of over ₹11,000 crore, one of the biggest in Indian banking history.
Another instance was the [YES BANK](https://in.linkedin.com/company/yes-bank?trk=public_post-text) crisis, where excessive exposure through off-balance sheet guarantees and commitments contributed to its downfall.
These cases made me realize that what remains off the balance sheet is not off the risk radar. Strong internal controls, transparency, and accountability are essential to prevent such misuse.
Key takeaway: In banking, what’s unseen can often be the most dangerous.

A. Draft Reserve Bank of India (Scheduled Commercial Banks - Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach) Directions, 2025
The proposed Directions seek to implement one of the key elements of the global reforms implemented by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), suitably tailored to the Indian context. The Directions amend the existing standardised approach framework for calculating the capital charge for credit risk with the objective of enhancing its robustness, granularity, and risk sensitivity.
The major revisions include:
nuanced and granular risk weight treatment for exposures to corporates, MSMEs and real estate;
inclusion of ‘transactors’ under regulatory retail category, where transactors are credit cards with timely repayments during the previous 12 months;
revision in the credit conversion factors for reckoning the exposure for off-balance sheet exposures;
suitable adjustments to the risk weights applied to loans rated by credit rating agencies, depending on the default history of such loans for each rating agency, and due diligence by banks.
Overall, the proposed changes are estimated to have a positive impact on the minimum regulatory capital requirements of banks, with certain segments such as MSMEs, real estate and credit cards exposures being particularly benefited.

# The Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021

RBI has integrated the three Ombudsman schemes namely, (i) the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006; (ii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies, 2018; and (iii) the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions, 2019; into one “The Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021”. The Scheme adopts ‘One Nation One Ombudsman’ approach by making the RBI Ombudsman mechanism jurisdiction neutral.

The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 is effective from November 12, 2021.

## **Salient Features****:**

1. Any customer aggrieved by deficiency in service (a shortcoming or an inadequacy in any financial service, which the Bank is required to provide statutorily or otherwise, which may or may not result in financial loss or damage to the customer) may file a complaint in writing or otherwise under the Scheme.
2. RBI has established the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre (CRPC) at Chandigarh for receipt of the complaints Pan India.
3. The complaint can be lodged through following modes –

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Online | **<https://cms.rbi.org.in>** |
| E-mail | crpc@rbi.org.in |
| Physical form in prescribed format (duly signed by complainant or by authorised representative) | ***Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, Reserve Bank of India, 4thFloor, Sector 17, Chandigarh – 160017*** |

**4.**Additionally, a Contact Centre with a **toll-free number – 14448 (9:30 am to 5:15 pm)** is available to provide information/clarifications regarding the alternate grievance redressal mechanism of RBI and to guide complainants in filing of a complaint.

**5.**A complaint under the Scheme shall not lie unless:

**(a).**the complainant had, before making a complaint under the Scheme, made a written complaint to the Bank concerned and

**(i).**the complaint was rejected wholly or partly by the Bank, and the complainant is not satisfied with the reply; or the complainant had not received any reply within 30 days after the Bank received the complaint; and

**(ii).**the complaint is made to the Ombudsman within one year after the complainant has received the reply from the Bank to the complaint or, where no reply is received, within one year and 30 days from the date of the complaint.

**(b).**the complaint is not in respect of the same cause of action which is already :

**(i).**pending before an Ombudsman or settled or dealt with on merits, by an Ombudsman, whether or not received from the same complainant or along with one or more complainants, or one or more of the parties concerned;

**(ii).**pending before any Court, Tribunal or Arbitrator or any other Forum or Authority; or, settled or dealt with on merits, by any Court, Tribunal or Arbitrator or any other Forum or Authority, whether or not received from the same complainant or along with one or more of the complainants/parties concerned;

(c)  the complaint is not abusive or frivolous or vexatious in nature;  
 (d) the complaint to the Bank was made before the expiry of the period of limitation prescribed under the Limitation Act, 1963, for such claims;  
 (e) the complainant provides complete information as specified in clause 11 of the Scheme;  
 (f) the complaint is lodged by the complainant personally or through an authorised representative other than an advocate unless the advocate is the aggrieved person.

**6.** No complaint for deficiency in service shall lie under the Scheme in matters involving:  
  (a) commercial judgment/commercial decision of a Bank;   
  (b) a dispute between a vendor and a Bank relating to an outsourcing contract;   
  (c) a grievance not addressed to the Ombudsman directly;   
  (d) general grievances against Management or Executives of a Bank;   
  (e) a dispute in which action is initiated by a Bank in compliance with the orders of a   statutory or law enforcing authority;   
  (f) a service not within the regulatory purview of the Reserve Bank;   
  (g) a dispute between Banks; and   
  (h) a dispute involving the employee-employer relationship of a Bank.

**7.** The complainant aggrieved by an Award or rejection of a complaint by Ombudsman Office may prefer an Appeal before the Appellate Authority within 30 days of the date of receipt of the Award or rejection of the complaint.   
 **8.** The Executive Director-in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department of RBI would be the Appellate Authority under the Scheme.  
 **9.** The Appellate Authority may, if it is satisfied that the complainant had sufficient cause for not making the appeal within the time, may allow a further period not exceeding 30 days.

* For more details, please refer to the Scheme details available on Bank’s website- ***www.upgb.bank.in*** or RBI’s website - ***www.rbi.org.in***.

* The copy of the Scheme is also available in our branch, which will be provided to the customer for reference upon request.
